hook_text: The Moon is always a perfect ball, half lit by the Sun. So why does it look like a banana one week and a coin the next?
clip_script: The Moon makes no light. It is a grey rock reflecting sunlight, and the Sun always lights exactly half of it. The trick is where we stand. At new Moon, it sits between us and the Sun, its bright side facing away: we see nothing. As it travels round us, we see a sliver of the lit half, then half of it, then nearly all. At full Moon, we are between it and the Sun, and the whole lit face shines back at us, rising at sunset. Then it shrinks back. One orbit, about a month. Try it tonight: one lamp, one white ball, turn slowly, and watch the phases appear in your hand.
visual_style: Whiteboard top-down view of the Sun on one side, Earth in the centre and eight Moons around it, each half shaded; beside each, the shape seen from Earth, from thin crescent to full circle.
pacing: Puzzle hook, a slow orbit, a hands-on challenge to finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and track the Moon for a month.
